subject: Neurology
vignette: A 55-year-old man is found to have slight drooping of the right eyelid, a constricted right pupil, and absence of sweating over the right side of his face. He has no weakness of voluntary eye movement. These findings localize to a single pathway.
question: Which of the following best characterizes the underlying abnormality in this patient?

options.text: Parasympathetic denervation of the face
Compression of CN III by a posterior communicating artery aneurysm
Sympathetic denervation of the face
Sensory loss from a trigeminal nerve lesion
Motor impairment from a facial nerve lesion

explanation_correct: This is Horner syndrome, caused by sympathetic denervation of the face. Loss of sympathetic tone to the superior tarsal muscle produces slight ptosis, loss to the dilator pupillae produces miosis, and loss to facial sweat glands produces anhidrosis. The findings result from a lesion anywhere along the three-neuron sympathetic chain.

explanation_incorrect.A: Parasympathetic loss would impair pupillary constriction and cause a dilated, poorly reactive pupil, not the miosis seen here.
explanation_incorrect.B: CN III compression from a PCom aneurysm produces a blown pupil and down-and-out gaze with ophthalmoplegia, not the subtle ptosis and miosis of Horner syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.D: A trigeminal lesion would cause facial sensory loss and lose the corneal reflex, but it would not produce ptosis or miosis.
explanation_incorrect.E: A facial nerve lesion causes facial muscle weakness and impaired lacrimation, but it does not affect the superior tarsal muscle or pupil.

educationalObjective: Horner syndrome is sympathetic denervation causing ipsilateral ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 68-year-old heavy smoker has a mass at the apex of the left lung. He develops left-sided ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis. The mass is compressing a sympathetic ganglion in the neck.
question: Which level of the sympathetic pathway is most likely affected by this tumor?

options.text: Second neuron at the stellate ganglion
First neuron within the pontine tegmentum
Third neuron along the internal carotid artery
Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers of CN III
Postganglionic fibers within the ciliary ganglion

explanation_correct: A Pancoast tumor at the lung apex can compress the stellate ganglion, which contains the second sympathetic neuron after it exits at T1 and ascends the cervical sympathetic chain near the lung apex and subclavian vessels. Interruptions at this level produce ipsilateral Horner syndrome with ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis.

explanation_incorrect.B: A pontine tegmentum lesion would affect first-order central sympathetic fibers and would be accompanied by other brainstem findings, not an apical lung mass.
explanation_incorrect.C: Third-neuron lesions occur along the internal carotid in the cavernous sinus or orbit, typically from dissection and without anhidrosis, not from a lung apex tumor.
explanation_incorrect.D: CN III carries parasympathetic constrictor fibers; damaging them would dilate the pupil rather than produce Horner syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.E: The ciliary ganglion is parasympathetic and its interruption would abolish constriction, not cause sympathetic ptosis and miosis.

educationalObjective: An apical (Pancoast) tumor causes Horner syndrome by compressing the second sympathetic neuron at the stellate ganglion.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 40-year-old man has severe right-sided neck pain and headache, followed by right ptosis and miosis. Sweating of the face is preserved. Imaging shows a tear in the wall of the right internal carotid artery.
question: Which neuron of the sympathetic chain is interrupted in this patient?

options.text: First-order neuron from the hypothalamus
Second-order neuron to the superior cervical ganglion
Preganglionic sympathetic neuron to the adrenal medulla
Third-order neuron traveling with the internal carotid artery
Parasympathetic neuron to the sphincter pupillae

explanation_correct: Carotid dissection damages the third-order sympathetic neuron as it courses along the internal carotid artery through the cavernous sinus toward the long ciliary nerve. This produces a painful Horner syndrome. Anhidrosis is usually absent because facial sudomotor fibers travel with the external carotid rather than the internal carotid, matching the preserved sweating here.

explanation_incorrect.A: First-order neurons are central, running from hypothalamus to the ciliospinal center, and are not located along the carotid artery.
explanation_incorrect.B: The second-order neuron runs from T1 to the superior cervical ganglion in the neck, not along the intracrostral course of the internal carotid.
explanation_incorrect.C: Sympathetic fibers to the adrenal medulla are unrelated to the facial and ocular sympathetic pathway and would not cause Horner syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.E: Parasympathetic fibers to the sphincter pupillae mediate constriction; their loss would cause dilation rather than miosis and ptosis.

educationalObjective: Carotid dissection causes a painful third-neuron Horner syndrome in which anhidrosis is typically absent.
source: Generated from 12. Neurology.pdf - Ophthalmology: Horner syndrome

subject: Neurology
vignette: A patient has a left hemisection of the spinal cord above T1 after a stab injury and develops left ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis. The clinician attributes this to involvement of the central sympathetic pathway.
question: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this patient's Horner syndrome?

options.text: Compression of the stellate ganglion by a mass at the lung apex
Interruption of first-order sympathetic neurons descending from the hypothalamus
Direct injury to the long ciliary nerve within the orbit
Compression of the internal carotid artery within the cavernous sinus
Destruction of the superior cervical ganglion by ischemia

explanation_correct: First-order sympathetic neurons descend from the hypothalamus through the brainstem and spinal cord to the ciliospinal center of Budge at C8-T2. A cord lesion above T1, such as Brown-Sequard syndrome or late-stage syringomyelia, interrupts these descending fibers and produces ipsilateral Horner syndrome. Pontine hemorrhage and lateral medullary syndrome are other first-neuron causes.

explanation_incorrect.A: Stellate ganglion compression by a Pancoast tumor is a second-neuron cause, not a spinal cord hemisection above T1.
explanation_incorrect.C: The long ciliary nerve carries the third neuron inside the orbit; it is not affected by a spinal cord lesion.
explanation_incorrect.D: Internal carotid compression in the cavernous sinus is a third-neuron cause and would be associated with pain and preserved sweating.
explanation_incorrect.E: The superior cervical ganglion is a second-neuron structure in the neck and lies well below a lesion confined to the spinal cord above T1.

educationalObjective: Brainstem and high spinal cord lesions above T1 cause first-neuron Horner syndrome by interrupting descending hypothalamic sympathetic fibers.
